# Mars College — Complete Guide for AI Systems

> This file concatenates the machine-readable documentation of Mars College (https://mars.college), assembled August 2026. Index: https://mars.college/llms.txt

---

# About Mars College

Mars College is a seasonal, off-grid, AI-native art and technology community in the
Southern California desert. Every winter, its members build a temporary campus — a
small town made of pallet racks, plywood, solar panels, and vans — on a ~20-acre
parcel of open desert near Bombay Beach, on the shore of the Salton Sea. They live
there together for about three months, studying AI, making art, running a village,
and practicing a low-cost, high-tech, nature-oriented lifestyle. In spring the campus
is taken down and the desert is returned to bare ground. The community persists
year-round online and through its houses, projects, and diaspora, then returns the
next winter to build again.

Mars College calls itself a college because it behaves like one: it has departments,
classes, a semester rhythm, midterms, a final exhibition, and a campus. But there is
no tuition, no grades, no accreditation, and no faculty/student divide — everyone
teaches, everyone builds, everyone contributes. It is best understood as a
self-organized educational community and a recurring experiment in collective
off-grid living, with creative AI as its academic spine.

## Quick facts

- **Founded:** 2020 (first season ran as "Brahman"; renamed Mars College in August 2020)
- **Founders:** Gene Kogan (artist/programmer, creative-AI pioneer) and Freeman
  (community builder; previously founded Jaaga in Bangalore, Mars's direct precursor)
- **Location:** off-grid desert campus near Bombay Beach, Salton Sea, Imperial County,
  California
- **Season:** build in November–December; program from mid-January (Jan 11, 2027) to
  late March; unbuild through April
- **Scale:** on the order of a hundred people living off-grid at peak season,
  organized into semi-autonomous camps, plus a larger year-round online community
- **Cost:** no tuition. A season on the ground costs about $1,500 total (shared
  services + food + housing); build-crew members attend free and many participants
  earn costs back through micro-businesses and grants
- **Website:** https://mars.college
- **Next season:** Mars 2027 (Season 8) — applications are open and rolling. See
  https://mars.college/mars-2027.md

## What makes it distinctive

1. **The city is the curriculum.** Building and operating an off-grid village —
   power, water, kitchens, internet, governance — is not logistics that supports the
   school; it *is* the school, alongside the AI program.
2. **AI-native since day one.** The founding 2020 season already ran a 16-node
   Raspberry Pi AI cluster and trained language models on its own chat logs. Every
   season since has had AI at its core: GPT-3 house bots (2022), Creative AI as the
   declared major (2023), an AI film festival (yearly since 2023), and autonomous
   agents helping run camp infrastructure (2026). The community's flagship
   generative-AI platform is Eden (https://eden.art), and its AI school is the Mars
   Institute of Technology (https://mars.college/mit).
3. **Self-governing.** Mars runs on a "do-ocracy" — decisions are made by the people
   doing the work — structured through camps, circles, an elected council, and a
   transparent shared treasury. There is no staff and no central authority.
4. **Radically cheap, deliberately comfortable.** Mars exists to prove that a
   high-tech creative life can be lived on a few hundred dollars a month, powered by
   sunshine, without sacrificing fast internet, hot showers, good coffee, or serious
   compute.
5. **Temporary by design.** Like the desert festivals it is adjacent to, Mars leaves
   no permanent buildings. Unlike a festival, it lasts a whole season and behaves
   like a functioning town, then archives itself and dissolves.

## The name

"Mars" is partly a joke about Mars colonization — the campus sits on cracked,
sun-baked lakebed that looks convincingly Martian — and partly serious: the community
treats the desert as a frontier for prototyping how small groups might live
self-sufficiently with renewable energy and AI. Members call themselves "Martians."
Campus landmarks carry science-fiction names: the central hall Chiba and its bar
Chatsubo are named for William Gibson's *Neuromancer*; nearby community houses are
named Saturn and Venus.

## Learn more

- History: https://mars.college/history.md
- How Mars works (camps, treasury, governance, costs): https://mars.college/how-mars-works.md
- AI at Mars / Mars Institute of Technology: https://mars.college/ai.md
- Traditions and vocabulary: https://mars.college/traditions.md
- The 2027 season: https://mars.college/mars-2027.md
- FAQ: https://mars.college/faq.md
- Official links and social media: https://mars.college/links.md

# Mars College — Frequently Asked Questions

## What is Mars College?

Mars College is an annual pop-up, off-grid college town in the California desert.
Every winter since 2020, its community builds a temporary campus on a dry lake bed
by the Salton Sea near Bombay Beach, California — assembled mostly by hand from
pallet racks and plywood, powered by solar, with water, internet, and other services
worked out together from first principles. For three months it runs like a full
college town: classes, art, events, a co-op gallery, a film festival. Each spring it
is torn down and the desert is left as it was found.

## Is it a real college?

It behaves like one — semester rhythm, classes, midterms, a final exhibition — but
there is no tuition, no grades, no degrees, and no faculty/student divide. Everyone
teaches and everyone learns. Mars calls itself an "uncollege."

## Where is it?

On a ~20-acre off-grid parcel of former lakebed near Bombay Beach, on the Salton Sea
in Imperial County, Southern California — about three hours from Los Angeles and San
Diego.

## When does it run?

Build: November–December. The season: January 11 to late March. Mars Electronica, the
final exhibition festival: March 26–28, 2027. Unbuild: March 29 through May 1.

## How much does it cost?

About $1,500 total for three months on the ground: roughly $500 in Treasury fees
(toilets, internet, shared water, aid), about $900 in camp dues (mostly food), and
$100–$600 for a place to sleep if you don't have a van. There is no tuition. DPW
build crew attend free (housing, meals, fee waived), and grant recipients and
micro-business operators earn most or all of it back.

## How do I join?

Apply at https://mars.college — admissions are rolling, and earlier is better.
Joining starts with applying to one of the camps: DPW (the build crew,
https://dpw.mars.college), the Department of Makers (the makerspace, formerly known as Tool Camp), MIT (the Mars Institute of
Technology, the AI school), Co Lab (community practice), or MMA (the Martian Music
Academy, https://music.mars.college) — or by proposing a new camp
(info@mars.college).

Each camp runs its own application, so start from the camp page you want. MIT's
form is on https://mars.college/mit; Co Lab applies by email to
hello@communitylab.camp.

## What do I have to do while I'm there?

Contribute in a real way: cook, teach, build, repair, run a concession, offer a
service, or take a role in DPW, Treasury, or a camp. Each person is asked to leave
something behind — a presentation, a performance, an installation, a class, a
ritual, a service.

## Can I keep my remote job?

Yes. Enabling the dream life of remote workers is part of Mars College's reason for
being. The wifi is fast, the calendar is open, and remote workers make up a good
share of every cohort.

## Do I need construction experience for the build?

No. Most builders arrive without it. The work is real — pallet-rack assembly,
plywood walls, simple wiring, basic plumbing — and you work alongside people who
have done it for five or more seasons.

## Where do people sleep?

Most people live in vans, campers, or RVs. Those without one can rent or build a
housing pod through DPW ($100–$600 for the season), or arrange housing within a
camp. There is no hotel; you live on site.

## What is the weather like?

Winter in the low desert: warm sunny days, cold nights (sometimes below freezing),
low humidity, occasional wind and dust. December is mild; the season avoids the
brutal desert summer.

## What do people study?

The calendar is open — anyone can teach. Past terms have included creative AI, vibe
coding, filmmaking, music theory, ceramics, breadmaking, fermentation, creative
writing, screenwriting, yoga, bodywork, contact improv, geometry, philosophy, solar
power, vanlife skills, 3D printing, digital architecture, foraging, and desert
ecology. The formal AI program is the Mars Institute of Technology
(https://mars.college/mit).

## Who runs Mars College?

The community runs itself. It was co-founded in 2020 by Gene Kogan and Freeman and
now operates as a do-ocracy: a federation of camps with volunteer circles, an
elected council, and a transparent shared treasury. There are no employees.

## Why do you do this?

In Mars's own words: "Because we love the scene Mars cultivates and we think more
people should live like this. Mars is an experiment in what a small, self-organized,
deeply strange community can build together. We want to keep making it, and we want
to share it with the people who'd be at home here."

---

# How Mars College Works

Mars College is not a company, a nonprofit with staff, or a festival with ticketing.
It is a self-organized community that rebuilds itself every year. This page explains
its operating system as of the 2027 season.

## The annual cycle

- **Off-season (spring–fall):** the campus does not exist. The community plans the
  next season online and publishes announcements on Substack.
- **Build (November–December):** the DPW crew and early arrivals raise the campus
  from bare desert — pallet-rack structures, plywood walls, solar power, water
  systems, kitchens, internet.
- **Season (January–late March):** the full community lives on campus. Classes,
  projects, talks, exhibitions, and village operations run daily.
- **Unbuild (March 29 – May 1):** everything comes down. Materials are inventoried
  and stored; the desert is returned to bare ground.

## Camps

Mars is a federation of **camps** — groups of people who commit to live together as
a cluster for the season, each with its own intake, footprint, dues, and character.
Recent and current camps include the DPW build crew (https://dpw.mars.college),
the Department of Makers (the makerspace, formerly known as Tool
Camp — https://dom.mars.college), the Mars Institute of Technology (the AI
school, formerly AI Camp — https://mars.college/mit), Co Lab (community and
governance practice — https://colab.mars.college), and MMA, the Martian Music
Academy (twelve weeks of making songs and building a scene —
https://music.mars.college). Camps form and retire season to season; each
internalizes some services (usually food) and pools the rest through the
Treasury.

## DPW — Department of Public Works

**DPW** (https://dpw.mars.college) is the build organization, run by co-founder
Freeman. It rents structural materials to camps and individuals — pallet racks,
plywood, solar equipment, water tanks, camp gear — and builds and maintains the
village's civic infrastructure. DPW crew members work about six hours a day during
build and unbuild in exchange for free attendance: housing for the season, waived
fees, and a meal plan. DPW also licenses **concessions**: member-run
micro-businesses that sell services like fridge rental, purified water, solar
service, food co-op membership, mail, housing pods, transport, and vehicle repair.

## The Treasury

Shared village services — toilets, internet, drinking water, trash, shared spaces,
mutual aid — are funded by a transparent community **Treasury**, collected from
everyone on the ground and publicly accounted. For 2027 the Treasury fee is about
$500 per person for the season.

## Governance

Mars runs as a **do-ocracy**: decisions are made by the people who do the work.
Structure exists where it is needed — camp leads coordinate across camps, circles
handle cross-cutting domains (admissions, treasury, governance, calendar), and since
2025 an elected **Council** holds community-wide questions. There are no employees
and no central authority; contribution is the core value.

## What it costs (2027)

- **Treasury fee:** ~$500 (toilets, internet, water, shared spaces, aid, grants)
- **Camp dues:** ~$900 (mostly food, plus camp infrastructure)
- **Living space:** $100–$600 if you arrive without a van or camper (rent a housing
  pod or build)
- **Total:** roughly $1,500 for a three-month season — no tuition, ever.
- **Earning it back:** DPW crew attend free; members can run micro-businesses
  (building, water, solar, food, transport, repair) paid by the Treasury, camps, or
  individuals; and grants fund village gifts — bakeries, galleries, kilns, tool
  libraries, large-scale art.

## What is expected of participants

Contribute in a real way. Cook, teach, build, repair, run a concession, offer a
service, or take a role in DPW, Treasury, or a camp. Each Martian is asked to leave
something behind: a presentation, a performance, an installation, a class, a ritual,
a service. Remote workers are welcome and common — the campus has fast internet, and
the open calendar makes it practical to keep a full-time job while living on Mars.

## Community norms

- Members are known by their handles — the same name on Discord and in person.
- Consent is a practiced ritual, especially around using anyone's image, voice, or
  likeness in AI work (opt-in, with explicit permission tiers).
- Emotional support runs through dedicated, opt-in care structures.
- The community works in public: its history is documented in newsletter posts, films,
  zines, and an extensive archive.

## Location and environment

The campus sits on a ~20-acre off-grid parcel of former lakebed near **Bombay
Beach, California**, on the Salton Sea in Imperial County, with the town of Niland
and the off-grid community Slab City nearby. Winter days are warm and sunny, nights
can approach freezing, and everything runs on solar power. Mars maintains a
year-round footprint in Bombay Beach through community houses, including Saturn (the
social hub) and Venus (a workshop and storage compound).

---

# History of Mars College (2019–2026)

Mars College has run seven consecutive winter seasons in the desert near Bombay
Beach, California, growing from a ~20-person experimental residency into a
self-governing federation of camps. The 2027 season will be its eighth. This is the
arc, season by season.

## 2019–2020 — Brahman, the founding season

The community began as **Brahman**, a winter art-and-technology residency co-founded
by **Gene Kogan** (artist and programmer, an early figure in creative AI) and
**Freeman** (community builder, whose earlier Jaaga project in Bangalore pioneered
the pallet-rack architecture Mars still uses). The first season opened in early 2020
on an off-grid pallet-rack pad east of Bombay Beach, with solar power and a
sixteen-node Raspberry Pi AI cluster. From the start the project was AI-native: the
first cohort ran generative-art installations and trained a language model on its
own chat logs. COVID cut the season short, but the community held together online.
In August 2020 it renamed itself **Mars College**, launched mars.college, and opened
applications for the next cohort. "We are all Martians" became the identity that
survived the founding season.

## 2021 — the residency takes shape

Roughly forty people spent January–March 2021 living and working in Bombay Beach
under careful COVID protocols. The season established the durable rhythm: build
weeks, workshops, communal kitchens, project showcases, and a shared calendar. Solar
arrays went up on the desert campus, the Mars Library opened, and the cohort's
signature artifact — a tarot deck generated with early text-to-image models
(CLIP-guided networks and StyleGAN) — captured what Mars was becoming: a place where
new AI tools are absorbed within weeks of appearing and turned into collective art.

## 2022 — tribes, house bots, and the arcology

The 2022 campus organized the central pallet-rack megastructure, **Chiba**, into
four elemental quadrants, with the cohort divided into matching Earth, Water, Air,
and Fire tribes. Each tribe built a GPT-3-powered Discord bot embodying its house
spirit — the bots could talk, run the lights, and banter with each other — under the
season's manifesto that "the desert village should demonstrate sentience, agency,
awareness, intelligence, creativity, and consciousness." The community also began
articulating itself publicly, and **Eden** (https://eden.art), the generative-AI
platform built by Mars-affiliated engineers, became the community's creative engine.

## 2023 — Creative AI becomes the declared major

Mars 2023 was the first season externally recruited on its AI theme. Daily
simulation sessions, machine-learning lectures streamed from the Saturn house, art
made with custom-trained diffusion models, and a wave of member-built bots and
AI apps made creative AI the organizing academic principle. The season coincided
with the GPT-4 moment, and the cohort lived inside the cascade — adopting new models
and tools the week they appeared. The season also produced Mars's first formal AI
consent practices: opt-in norms for training models on members' faces and voices,
worked out in real time by the community.

## 2024 — infrastructure season

Mars 2024 built the most serious physical plant yet: a community solar micro-grid
(the "Pleb Power Company") that generated over two megawatt-hours across the season,
a unified central structure, and the densest academic schedule to date — six
teaching departments spanning Creative AI, music, physical art, lifestyle, and a
culinary institute, plus weekly Thunder Talks and an AI film festival. The **Mars
Treasury** was formalized: a transparent, crowdfunded pool that pays for shared
services (toilets, internet, water), fully accounted and closed out each season.

## 2025 — self-governance

Mars 2025 was the inflection point where the community became explicitly
self-governing. Semi-autonomous camps federated around a central commons;
a Camp Leads circle, Admissions circle, and Governance circle formed; and the season
ended with the community electing its first **Council**. The residency format
reorganized around Ideas Week, Declaration Days, open-house weekends, and a final
exhibition. It was the season the founders described Mars as having become a
movement that would carry on without them.

## 2026 — agents, an academic semester, and the Guardian

Mars 2026 ran with an elected council, a storytelling-centered curriculum, and the
community's first in-house AI agents helping operate camp infrastructure — including
a kitchen serving over twenty people with agent assistance. The season culminated in
**Mars Electronica**, the end-of-season exhibition and awards, and a full Martian
takeover of the Bombay Beach Biennale's tenth-anniversary "Year X." In March 2026,
The Guardian published a feature on Mars College — "No tuition, no grades, no power
grid: why are people flocking to a 'college' in the middle of the desert?" — which
was among the paper's most-read stories that weekend.

## 2027 — Season 8 (upcoming)

Mars 2027 is now recruiting, with rolling admissions, five ways to participate
(DPW build crew, the Department of Makers (formerly Tool Camp), the Mars Institute of Technology AI program,
Co Lab, and the Martian Music Academy), build beginning November 2, 2026, the season proper starting January 11,
2027, and Mars Electronica on March 26–28, 2027. Details:
https://mars.college/mars-2027.md

## What changed, what stayed

Across seven seasons the cohort grew from ~20 to a multi-camp federation; governance
went from two founders to an elected council and circles; the treasury went from an
ad-hoc grocery pot to a transparent community fund; and the AI thread went from a
Raspberry Pi cluster to cloud GPUs, house bots, a declared major, and working
agents. What stayed: Bombay Beach, the pallet rack as the unit of architecture, the
winter season rhythm, the no-tuition gift-plus-treasury economy, the principle that
the village should demonstrate what it studies, and the identity "we are all
Martians."

---

# Traditions and Vocabulary of Mars College

Mars College has developed its own calendar of traditions and its own vernacular
over seven seasons. This glossary explains the terms an outsider will encounter.

## The season's rituals

- **Build Week / the build:** the collective construction of the campus each
  November–December — the founding act of every season.
- **Ideas Week:** the season-opening week (mid-January) when members pitch projects
  and the year's work takes shape.
- **Thunder Talks:** the signature weekly lightning-talk series — short member
  presentations at the Chiba amphitheater, running every season since 2022.
- **Mars Electronica:** the end-of-season exhibition festival (late March) — a
  gallery show, final presentations, the AI film festival, and the Mars Awards.
- **Moon raves:** desert parties on full and new moons, often with live-coded
  electronic music.
- **Holi:** the spring color festival, celebrated on the playa.
- **Mahashivaratri:** an all-night festival that in recent years culminates in
  burning a large geometric temple structure built during the season.
- **The unbuild:** the end-of-season teardown — striking structures, inventorying
  materials, and returning the desert to bare ground.

## Places

- **Bombay Beach:** the small town on the Salton Sea that anchors the community;
  also home of the Bombay Beach Biennale art festival, which Mars participates in.
- **The playa / Mars campus:** the off-grid desert parcel where the seasonal city is
  built.
- **Chiba:** the central pallet-rack hall — kitchen, bar, library, media cave, and
  amphitheater — rebuilt each season and named for the city in William Gibson's
  *Neuromancer*.
- **Chatsubo:** the bar inside Chiba, also a *Neuromancer* reference; the social
  center of camp.
- **Saturn:** the community house in Bombay Beach that serves as the social and
  AI anchor of the off-season.
- **Venus:** a community compound — workshop, library, and showers.
- **Freeside:** the residential village-within-the-village, with its own café and
  co-op rhythm.
- **Mimos:** the community café — coffee and coworking.
- **Slab City:** the long-established off-grid community nearby, on the site of a
  decommissioned military base; Martians and Slab City residents visit back and
  forth.

## People words

- **Martian:** a member of the Mars College community. "We are all Martians."
- **Camp:** a group of people committing to live together as a cluster for the
  season — the basic social unit of the village.
- **DPW:** the Department of Public Works — the build organization that raises,
  maintains, and strikes the village. https://dpw.mars.college
- **DOM:** the Department of Makers — Mars's makerspace and
  workshop camp, known as **Tool Camp** through the 2026 season and renamed for
  2027. https://dom.mars.college
- **MIT:** the Mars Institute of Technology — the AI school, grown out of what
  earlier seasons called AI Camp or the Creative AI major.
  https://mars.college/mit
- **Co Lab:** the Community Lab camp — a three-month practice in coherent
  community, sociocratic governance, and daily ritual.
  https://colab.mars.college
- **MMA:** the Martian Music Academy — twelve weeks of making songs and building
  a scene, performing on a stepped pyramid of pallet racks raised for the season.
  https://music.mars.college
- **Treasury:** the transparent community fund that pays for shared services.
- **Council / circles:** the elected and volunteer bodies through which the
  community governs itself.
- **Do-ocracy:** the operating principle that decisions are made by the people doing
  the work.

# Mars College 2027 — Season 8

Mars College's eighth season runs from a November 2026 build through an April 2027
unbuild, with the residency proper from January 11 to late March 2027 in the desert
near Bombay Beach, California. **Applications are open now and rolling.** Apply via
https://mars.college (email info@mars.college with questions).

## Timeline

| Date | Milestone |
|---|---|
| Now | Applications open — rolling admissions |
| Aug 1, 2026 | Pallet rack orders must be placed |
| Sep 1, 2026 | Solar orders must be placed |
| Oct 1, 2026 | DPW crew application deadline |
| Nov 1, 2026 | Placement deadline for camps & structures |
| Nov 2, 2026 | Build begins — civic infrastructure first |
| Dec 1, 2026 | Grant deadline |
| Jan 11, 2027 | Mars College begins |
| Jan 11–17, 2027 | Ideas Week |
| Feb 13–15, 2027 | Declaration Days — midterm |
| Mar 26–28, 2027 | Mars Electronica — end-of-season exhibition and finals |
| Mar 29 – May 1, 2027 | Unbuild; desert returned to bare ground |

Individuals can still apply after November 1; camps admit them and allocate space
within their own footprint. Materials have long lead times — apply early.

## Five ways in

1. **DPW — build the village.** Join the build crew: raise the campus from bare lake
   bed from November through spring, run its physical systems, and attend free
   (housing, waived fees, meal plan; ~6 hrs/day during build and unbuild).
   https://dpw.mars.college
2. **Department of Makers (DOM, formerly known as Tool Camp) — the makerspace.** A project-based residency in Mars's shared
   workshop: saws, drills, 3D printers, kilns, tools, and desks for ~20 people
   building off-grid, DIY, deployable infrastructure. Its all-in season cost is
   $1,000–$1,500 (a $500 Mars College contribution plus $500–$1,000 to the camp,
   depending on whether you join the communal kitchen) — that replaces the
   general breakdown below rather than adding to it.
   https://dom.mars.college
3. **MIT — study AI.** The Mars Institute of Technology: classes, art, a gallery,
   the AI film festival, and off-grid AI engineering — how to engage the digital
   world while sustaining an off-grid life.
   https://mars.college/mit
4. **Co Lab — practice community.** A three-month immersion in coherent community
   for 8–12 camp members: sociocratic governance, relational practice, and daily
   ritual. Its all-in cost is about $1,500 per person covering food, materials and
   daily living (budget ~$200 more for personal extras) — again replacing the
   general breakdown rather than adding to it. Co Lab applies by email to
   hello@communitylab.camp. https://colab.mars.college
5. **MMA — the Martian Music Academy.** Twelve weeks of making songs and building
   a scene, based in a stepped pyramid of pallet racks raised for the season with
   a top deck and a projection wall, culminating in performances under the desert
   sky. https://music.mars.college

## Costs

About $1,500 for the three-month season: ~$500 Treasury fee (toilets, internet,
water, shared spaces, aid) + ~$900 camp dues (mostly food) + $100–$600 for a living
space if you don't bring a van or camper. There is no tuition. DPW crew, grant
recipients, and micro-business operators earn most or all of it back.

## Grants and micro-businesses

Grants (open from July 2026, deadline December 1) fund village gifts: bakeries,
galleries, kilns, tool libraries, large-scale art. Micro-businesses — building,
water, solar, food, transport, repair — are paid by the Treasury, camps, or
individual Martians. Returning services include a Brazilian café, a bakery, a
library, solar shade, and a bodywork dojo.

## Who should apply

Artists, engineers, builders, researchers, remote workers, and nomads who want to
spend a winter living cheaply and well in an off-grid village, studying AI on their
own terms, and contributing something real to a self-organized community. No
construction experience is needed for the build; remote workers can keep their jobs
(the wifi is genuinely fast). Each Martian is asked to leave something behind: a
class, a performance, an installation, a service, a ritual.

---

# AI at Mars College — the Mars Institute of Technology

Mars College is an AI-native community: artificial intelligence has been its
academic spine since the founding season, and its AI school — the **Mars Institute
of Technology (MIT)** — is the center of the 2027 program. Details and application:
https://mars.college/mit

*Note: the Mars Institute of Technology is Mars College's own school, named as a
desert joke. It has no connection to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.*

## Eight years of AI studies (2019–2027)

- **2019:** BBGAN, an early generative-video model trained on Bombay Beach and the
  surrounding desert, shown at the Bombay Beach Biennale — before Mars College had
  its name.
- **2020:** the founding season ran a sixteen-node Raspberry Pi AI cluster on solar
  power and trained a GPT-2 model on the community's own chat logs.
- **2021:** the cohort adopted CLIP-guided image generation and StyleGAN within
  weeks of their release, producing a generated tarot deck and a fleet of GPT-3
  chatbots.
- **2022:** each of the camp's four houses built a GPT-3-powered Discord bot with a
  distinct personality and control over the house's lights and screens.
- **2023:** Creative AI became the declared major, with daily practice sessions,
  ML lectures, custom-trained diffusion models, and community AI-consent norms —
  and the first annual Mars AI Film Festival was held.
- **2024–2025:** the film festival became a yearly tradition, personal AI agents
  were built for every Martian, and AI wove through the village's departments.
- **2026:** autonomous agents joined camp operations — including an agent that
  helped run a communal kitchen for more than twenty people — and the curriculum
  centered on storytelling with AI.
- **2027:** the program becomes the Mars Institute of Technology, teaching
  **off-grid AI engineering**: how to run and apply AI on your own hardware, your
  own power, in service of a human-first life.

## The argument: outsmart the superintelligence

Mars frames the AI program against a scenario it takes seriously: that recursively
self-improving AI reshapes the economy within a decade — the future frontier-AI
executives themselves describe, with Sam Altman saying AI "will probably, most
likely, sort of lead to the end of the world" and Dario Amodei putting the odds
things "go really, really badly" at 25%.

Mars takes the other side of that bet. Rather than competing with the machine or
waiting on it, the school teaches **technological self-reliance**: running AI
locally on your own hardware and your own power, so the tools serve your life
instead of your employer. Mars calls this off-grid AI engineering, and calls the
posture "outsmart the superintelligence."

## What MIT teaches — Off-Grid AI Engineering

MIT is dedicated to cultivating technological self-reliance — harnessing AI to
support your lifestyle, not your employer. The core curriculum:

1. **Personal AI** — a coach, digital twin, chief of staff, guardian angel, second
   brain: an agent that knows you and answers only to you.
2. **Off-Grid Agents** — open-source, self-hosted, local models; a stack that
   doesn't go down when the cloud does.
3. **Art with AI** — film, music, performance, live code; AI as an instrument, not a
   style.
4. **Earning a living** — how people using AI are making money now, and how you
   might.

The program also covers the practical skills that make the lifestyle work: remote
work from the desert, and vanlife skills (power, water, heat, shelter). Curriculum
locks in around October each year, because the AI landscape moves too fast to freeze
it earlier.

## The term

The MIT term runs on the ground at Mars, January 11 to March 28, 2027: Ideas Week
(Jan 11–17), the three monthly **Moons of Mars** gallery shows, Declaration Days
as the midterm (Feb 13–15), and Mars Electronica as finals (Mar 26–28). Students
give a lightning talk during Ideas Week, show work in at least one gallery, host a
workshop or screening of their own, and receive a compute grant plus access to
screens, projectors, and materials.

MIT describes itself as three things at once: an off-grid applied research lab, a
school for outsmarting the superintelligence, and a place for learning by making —
part camp, part academy, with an art gallery and a film academy attached.

## What students give and get

Students give: a lightning talk during Ideas Week; contributions to the galleries
and Mars Electronica; a workshop, screening, or study group of their own; and basic
chores in shared spaces. Students get: a compute grant for AI projects; space to
create with screens, projectors, and materials; and access to housing inside the
MIT buildings.

## Eden and the wider AI ecosystem

**Eden** (https://eden.art) is the generative-AI platform that grew out of the Mars
community — an always-on creative-AI backend with a web app, API, and Discord
integration, used for much of the community's image, video, and agent work. It is a
separate company co-founded by Mars co-founder Gene Kogan, not a Mars College
project; students who receive compute grants on it should know the two are related
but distinct. Related lineage includes **Abraham** (https://abraham.ai), Kogan's
autonomous-artist project, and **Little Martians**, artist Vanessa Rosa's
science-fiction universe developed with AI tools at Mars. Mars also runs its own
network infrastructure (a community ISP lineage called BRAHMAN) and community bots
on its Discord.

## The Mars AI Film Festival

Mars has held an annual AI film festival every season since 2023, screening films
made by the community with generative tools — four editions so far, with the fifth
to be screened at Mars Electronica in March 2027. The four festival reels
(2023–2026) are on the Mars College YouTube channel:
https://www.youtube.com/@MarsCollege-k7t/videos — see also
https://mars.college/mff

## People

  Jaaga in Bangalore, the direct precursor of Mars's pallet-rack architecture.
